questions.question: What is a list in Python, and how does list mutability work?
questions.title: Python List Basics and Mutability
questions.direct_answer: A Python list is an ordered, mutable sequence that can hold values of different types and keep duplicates. Mutability means operations such as item assignment, `append`, and `remove` can change the same list object, so every name that refers to that object can observe the change.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand list order, mutation, aliases, and the difference between changing an object and creating another list.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying `alias = items` copies a list, or assigning the result of `items.append(x)` back to `items`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use object identity to explain why aliases observe the same append and why a shallow copy creates only a new outer list.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A list is ordered: each item has a position and iteration follows that order.
A list is mutable: its contents can change without creating a new list object.
Lists allow duplicate values and may contain values of different types.
Assignment can create an alias; use `copy()` or slicing when a separate outer list is needed.
Methods that only mutate a list, such as `append()` and `sort()`, return `None`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Python list is an ordered, mutable sequence. Each item has a zero-based position, iteration follows that order, duplicate values are allowed, and the list can grow or shrink. A list may legally contain different types, although keeping related values together usually makes the model and its operations easier to understand.

Mutability means the same list object can change its contents. `tasks.append("test")` adds a position, `tasks[0] = "design"` replaces one stored reference, and `tasks.remove("test")` removes an item. By contrast, `tasks + ["deploy"]` constructs another list and leaves the original object unchanged unless its name is rebound.

Assignment does not copy a list. After `alias = tasks`, both names refer to one object, so an append through `alias` is visible through `tasks`. Passing the list to a function follows the same reference rule. This can be intentional shared state, but it becomes a bug when the caller expected independent ownership.

`tasks.copy()` or `tasks[:]` creates a different outer list, so later appends and removals on that outer container are isolated. The copy is shallow: nested lists or dictionaries are still the same objects. Copying solves only the ownership level it actually duplicates, so nested edits need their own copy or deliberate reconstruction.

Choose a list when position, iteration order, duplicates, or later structural updates are part of the requirement. Use a set when unique membership is the main relationship and a dictionary when a stable key should find a value directly. Mutating methods such as `append()` and `sort()` return `None`, which makes it clear that they change the list rather than create a replacement result.

sections.title: A list is an object with positions
sections.content:
A list stores references in a numbered sequence. The first position is index `0`, and the last can be reached with index `-1`. Changing an element replaces the reference held at one position; appending adds another position. The list object itself can keep the same identity through both operations.

That reference model explains aliasing. Two variables can lead to the same list, and Python does not silently copy it during assignment or when it is passed to a function. Copy only when the ownership rule says that later structural changes must be isolated.

sections.title: One mutation, two aliases
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[name: tasks] --> L["one list: ['plan']"]
  B[name: alias] --> L
  M["alias.append('test')"] --> U["same list: ['plan', 'test']"]
  L --> U
```

Both names lead to the same object, so the append is visible from either name.

sections.title: Observe identity and an independent copy
sections.content:
```python
tasks = ["plan"]
alias = tasks
separate = tasks.copy()

alias.append("test")
separate.append("review")

print(tasks)            # ['plan', 'test']
print(alias is tasks)   # True
print(separate)         # ['plan', 'review']
print(separate is tasks)  # False
```

questions.question: How do indexing and slicing work in Python lists?
questions.title: Python List Indexing and Slicing
questions.direct_answer: Indexing selects one list item and raises `IndexError` when the position is outside the list. Slicing uses `[start:stop:step]`, includes `start`, excludes `stop`, accepts negative positions, and returns a new shallow list containing references to the selected items.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can predict positive and negative indexes, half-open slice bounds, steps, and the allocation boundary of a slice.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating the stop index as included, or assuming a slice recursively copies nested objects.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Translate `[start:stop:step]` into a directional walk and distinguish clipped slice bounds from failing single-index access.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Index `0` is the first item, while `-1` is the last item.
A slice includes `start` but excludes `stop`: `items[1:4]` selects positions 1, 2, and 3.
Omitted bounds mean the available beginning or end; the default step is `1`.
A negative step walks backward, so `items[::-1]` returns a reversed shallow copy.
A normal out-of-range index fails, but slice bounds are clipped to the sequence.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Indexing selects exactly one item. Python lists use zero-based positions, so `items[0]` is the first element. A single index must identify an available position; asking for one outside the list raises `IndexError`. Direct list indexing is constant-time access and does not allocate another list.

A negative index counts backward from the end: `items[-1]` is the final item, `items[-2]` is the one before it, and so on. It is still a single-position lookup, so a negative index that reaches beyond the beginning also raises `IndexError`.

A slice uses `items[start:stop:step]`. Python begins at `start`, repeatedly moves by `step`, and stops before reaching `stop` in that direction. The start is included and the stop is excluded, so `letters[1:4]` selects positions `1`, `2`, and `3`. A step of zero is invalid because the walk could never advance.

Omitted bounds use the reachable beginning or end, and the default step is `1`. A negative step walks backward, which is why `items[::-1]` returns a reversed result. Slice bounds beyond the list are clipped instead of raising `IndexError`, making slices useful for chunks and pages even near an outer boundary.

A list slice returns a new outer list containing references to the selected items, and its cost grows with the number of selected references. It is a shallow copy: if an item is itself a list, changing that nested object through the slice is visible in the original. Use an index for one required item and a slice for a natural subsequence.

beats.spokenText: Indexing selects exactly one item. Python lists use zero-based positions, so `items[0]` is the first element. support.title: Run positive, stepped, reverse, and shallow slices
support.code:
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
print(letters[0], letters[-1])
print(letters[1:4])
print(letters[::2])
print(letters[::-1])

nested = [[1], [2]]
part = nested[:]
part[0].append(9)

support.caption: The slice has its own outer list, while the nested list at position zero remains shared.

beats.recallRule: An index selects one position; a slice walks from an included start to an excluded stop and returns a shallow list.

sections.title: Slice boundaries and step direction
sections.content:
The colon form describes a walk, not two included indexes. Python begins at `start`, repeatedly adds `step`, and stops before it would reach or pass `stop` in the direction of travel. That rule works for both positive and negative steps. A step of zero is invalid because the walk could never advance.

Slicing is forgiving at the outer bounds, which is useful for chunking and pagination. It still allocates another list proportional to the number of selected references. A direct index is constant-time access and does not allocate a result list.

sections.title: The half-open slice `[1:4]`
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I0["0 · a"] --> I1["1 · b · start"] --> I2["2 · c"] --> I3["3 · d"] --> I4["4 · e · stop"]
  I1 -. selected .-> I2
  I2 -. selected .-> I3
```

The stop boundary marks where selection ends; the item at index `4` is not included.

sections.title: Trace indexes, slices, and a shallow boundary
sections.content:
```python
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
print(letters[0], letters[-1])  # a e
print(letters[1:4])             # ['b', 'c', 'd']
print(letters[::2])             # ['a', 'c', 'e']
print(letters[::-1])            # ['e', 'd', 'c', 'b', 'a']

nested = [[1], [2]]
part = nested[:]
part[0].append(9)
print(nested)                    # [[1, 9], [2]]
```

questions.question: What is the difference between `append`, `extend`, `insert`, `remove`, `pop`, and `del` on a Python list?
questions.title: Python List Methods Compared
questions.direct_answer: `append` adds one object, `extend` adds every item from an iterable, and `insert` adds one object at a chosen position. `remove` deletes the first equal value, `pop` removes and returns an item, while `del` deletes by index or slice without returning the removed data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you choose a list operation from one item versus an iterable, value versus position, and whether the removed item is needed.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `append` when the iterable's elements should be added, or expecting `remove` to return the deleted value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Include the shifting cost near the front and name `deque` for a real queue with frequent left-end operations.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `append(x)` adds `x` as one final element, even when `x` is itself a list.
`extend(iterable)` appends each item produced by the iterable.
`insert(i, x)` places one value before position `i` and shifts later items.
`remove(x)` deletes the first equal value and raises `ValueError` when it is absent.
`pop(i)` removes and returns an item; `pop()` uses the final item by default.
`del items[i:j]` removes positions or a slice and produces no return value.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`append(x)` puts `x` at the end as one new list element. If `x` is itself `[3, 4]`, that entire list becomes one nested element. `append` mutates the existing list and returns `None`; assigning its result back to the list therefore loses the list reference.

`extend(values)` iterates over `values` and appends each produced item. Starting with `[1, 2]`, extending with `[3, 4]` produces `[1, 2, 3, 4]`, while appending the same value produces `[1, 2, [3, 4]]`. Strings are iterable too, so extending with `"ab"` adds two characters.

`insert(i, x)` adds one object before position `i`. Existing references from that position onward shift to the right, so insertion near the front takes linear time. It is useful for occasional positional edits, but repeated left-end queue operations need a structure designed for both ends.

`remove(x)` searches by equality and deletes the first matching value; it returns `None` and raises `ValueError` when no match exists. `pop(i)` removes by position and returns the item; `pop()` uses the final position and an empty list raises `IndexError`. `del` is a statement that deletes an index or slice without returning the removed data.

Appending and popping at the right edge are amortized `O(1)`, while inserting or deleting near the front is `O(n)` because later references shift. Use `collections.deque` for a real queue with frequent left-end work. `clear()` removes every item while keeping the same list object. Choose from one object, an iterable, a value, or a position rather than from method names alone.

beats.cue: Define append as adding exactly one object
beats.spokenText: `append(x)` puts `x` at the end as one new list element. If `x` is itself `[3, 4]`, that entire list becomes one nested element. `append` mutates the existing list and returns `None`; assigning its result back to the list therefore loses the list reference.

beats.cue: Define extend as consuming an iterable
beats.spokenText: `extend(values)` iterates over `values` and appends each produced item. Starting with `[1, 2]`, extending with `[3, 4]` produces `[1, 2, 3, 4]`, while appending the same value produces `[1, 2, [3, 4]]`. Strings are iterable too, so extending with `"ab"` adds two characters.

beats.cue: Place insert at a selected position
beats.spokenText: `insert(i, x)` adds one object before position `i`. Existing references from that position onward shift to the right, so insertion near the front takes linear time. It is useful for occasional positional edits, but repeated left-end queue operations need a structure designed for both ends.

beats.cue: Separate removal by value from removal by position
beats.spokenText: `remove(x)` searches by equality and deletes the first matching value; it returns `None` and raises `ValueError` when no match exists. `pop(i)` removes by position and returns the item; `pop()` uses the final position and an empty list raises `IndexError`. `del` is a statement that deletes an index or slice without returning the removed data.

items.label: pop(i)

items.label: del items[i:j]

beats.cue: Connect method choice to result shape and cost
beats.spokenText: Appending and popping at the right edge are amortized `O(1)`, while inserting or deleting near the front is `O(n)` because later references shift. Use `collections.deque` for a real queue with frequent left-end work. `clear()` removes every item while keeping the same list object. Choose from one object, an iterable, a value, or a position rather than from method names alone.

support.title: See addition and removal create different shapes
support.code:
values = [1, 2]
values.append([3, 4])
print(values)

flat = [1, 2]
flat.extend([3, 4])
flat.insert(1, 9)
print(flat)

flat.remove(9)
last = flat.pop()
del flat[:1]
print(last, flat)
support.caption: `append` nests one list, `extend` adds its items, and the removal operations differ in whether they return data.

beats.recallRule: Add one object with `append`, consume many with `extend`, remove by value with `remove`, and remove-and-return by position with `pop`.

sections.title: Addition and removal use different coordinates
sections.content:
A list can be addressed by position or searched by value. `insert`, `pop`, and `del` use positions; `remove` performs an equality search to find a value. That is why `remove` can fail even when the index would be valid, and why duplicate values make it remove only the first match.

At the right edge, the internal array normally has room for efficient growth, so repeated appends are amortized constant time. Work at the left edge shifts existing references. A deque changes the storage model to make both ends efficient, but it gives up arbitrary slicing.

sections.title: Match the method to the intent
sections.content:
| Operation | Selects by | Adds/removes | Returns removed value? | Typical cost |
|---|---|---|---:|---|
| `append(x)` | one object | add at end | No | amortized O(1) |
| `extend(xs)` | iterable | add at end | No | O(len(xs)) |
| `insert(i, x)` | position | add before `i` | No | O(n) |
| `remove(x)` | value equality | first match | No | O(n) |
| `pop()` | final position | remove | Yes | O(1) |
| `del items[i:j]` | position/slice | remove | No | O(n) |

sections.title: See the operations produce different shapes
sections.content:
```python
values = [1, 2]
values.append([3, 4])
print(values)  # [1, 2, [3, 4]]

flat = [1, 2]
flat.extend([3, 4])
flat.insert(1, 9)
print(flat)    # [1, 9, 2, 3, 4]

flat.remove(9)
last = flat.pop()
del flat[:1]
print(last)    # 4
print(flat)    # [2, 3]
```

followup_questions: Why is `append` described as amortized O(1)?

Why is `deque.popleft()` preferable to `list.pop(0)` for a queue?
